source.title: Ridgeless Regression with Random Features
source.authors: Jian Li; Yong Liu; Yingying Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps random-feature dimension and measures test error, testing double descent in a non-deep model class with a different method and setting from the original deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: The test-error sweeps over random-feature dimension and the reported test-error trajectories over epochs are included. Results cited from other studies, hyperparameter choices used only for tuning, and classification accuracy comparisons in Table 1 are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: Figure 2(a) sweeps random Fourier feature count M at fixed n under three ridge levels and reports test error. This repeats the random-Fourier-feature sweep in Belkin et al. (an original source of V4), adds a regularization comparison, and gives a variance-explosion account. The epoch plots never show a fall-rise-fall curve, so V2 is not effectively tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors show, in theory and on one plotted sweep, that ridgeless random-feature error peaks at M=n because variance explodes there. For M<n, random features act as implicit ridge with λ shrinking as M grows; for M>n, error descends toward the ridgeless kernel predictor. The curve is more obvious with smaller explicit regularization. They also bound SGD error by b, γ and t, and propose RFTK, which penalizes Tr(K).
record.recipe_differences: Studies ridgeless kernel regression with random Fourier features and SGD, varying feature dimension and regularization rather than scaling deep networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The double-descent curve is described as more obvious with smaller regularization. SGD error and test MSE vary with batch size, learning rate, and training duration.
record.peer_reviewed: International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI)
record.problems: The central double-descent test-error values are presented in plots without numerical values in the text. The sample count for the Figure 2(a) dimension sweep is not stated. The epoch plots do not establish a complete fall-rise-fall trajectory.

untested.parts: No deep networks; only random-feature models are swept.
No epoch-wise fall-rise-fall curve is reported; the epoch plots show convergence or a late accuracy decline only.
No single complexity measure predicting peak location across axes. Effective dimension appears only in the theory for M<n.
No label-noise sweep, no multiple descent, and no test of peak disappearance under optimally tuned ridge.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: The dataset, n, and noise level for the Figure 2(a) M/n sweep are not stated, so the setting of the double-descent rows cannot be pinned down.
missing.locator: Section 6.1, Double Descent Curve in Random Features; Figure 2(a)

missing.what: Kernel (M→∞) predictor test errors at each λ are plotted as dashed reference lines; these could serve as baselines for rows r1–r3.

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed because random features are not deep networks. The study is mainly theoretical; its double-descent evidence is one figure with no numbers in the text. Belkin et al. (an original) already showed random-Fourier-feature double descent, so this is close to a T1 replication for V4. Table 1 accuracies are method comparisons and correctly have no rows.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and other model-size measures are not tested; the study varies random-feature dimension.
The study reports epoch trajectories for random-feature methods, not deep networks, and does not establish a fall-rise-fall curve over epochs.
No sweep over training sample size near the interpolation threshold is reported.
The empirical test is limited to random-feature regression; other model classes are not swept.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study discusses variance and varies regularization, but does not sweep label noise, test triple or multiple descent, or establish disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No comparison against an effective parameter count or demonstration that this transforms the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: ridgeless RF predictor
rows.size_stated: random features dimension M; sample count n not stated for this plot
rows.operation_detail: Reported the variance factor α as a function of M/n.
rows.note: The text says the variance factor grows near M=n and that variance explodes at the interpolation point.
rows.check: The plotted α is the analytical constant from the bound (α ∝ M/(M−n) or n/(n−M)), not a measured variance. It is theoretical support for a variance-driven peak, not an empirical result.

rows.subject: RF-SGD
rows.locator: Figure 2(b); Section 6.1, Benefits from Tunable Kernel
rows.note: The reported late accuracy decline indicates increasing test error after 100 epochs, but the text does not establish a complete fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: Accuracy declines after 100 epochs, which the authors attribute to overfitting. No second descent is shown within 200 epochs, and test accuracy is not the version's test error.

rows.subject: RFTK
rows.operation_detail: Reported test accuracy during training while optimizing the spectral density.
rows.value: more iterations can still improve generalization performance
rows.locator: Figure 2(b)-(c); Section 6.1, Benefits from Tunable Kernel
rows.note: This method continuously optimizes its kernel during training; the report does not establish a fall-rise-fall test-error curve.
rows.check: RFTK is the authors' own method, whose kernel changes during training. This is a method-performance result, not a test of epoch-wise double descent.

relationships.condition: Ridgeless or lightly regularized random Fourier feature regression, test error vs M/n
relationships.reason: Error falls, peaks at M=n, and falls again for M>n toward the kernel predictor (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Test error initially fell, peaked at M=n, and declined again for M>n toward the kernel predictor.

relationships.reason: The peak is most pronounced when ridgeless and weakens as λ grows (r1–r3). The theory attributes the peak to variance explosion at M=n, but r9 is analytical, not measured.
relationships.display_finding: The peak was strongest without ridge and weakened as λ increased, while theory attributed it to variance exploding at M=n.
